title: Bullous Keratopathy: The Endothelial Failure Masterclass
summary: A comprehensive clinical breakdown of corneal endothelial decompensation, ranging from Pseudophakic Bullous Keratopathy (PBK) to Fuchs' Dystrophy. This guide covers pathophysiology, advanced imaging, and the evolution of lamellar keratoplasty.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Bullous Keratopathy (BK) is a pathological condition characterized by the formation of epithelial bullae (blisters) resulting from chronic corneal edema. This occurs when the corneal endothelial cell density falls below a critical threshold (typically <500 cells/mm²), failing to maintain the cornea's relative state of dehydration (deturgescence). It is most commonly seen following cataract surgery (PBK) or as the end-stage of Fuchs' Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy (FECD).

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Pump vs. Leak Mechanism
content: Step 1: Endothelial cell loss due to surgical trauma, genetic dystrophy, or high IOP.
Step 2: Failure of the Na+/K+ ATPase 'pump' mechanism and breakdown of 'leaky' tight junctions.
Step 3: Aqueous humor enters the corneal stroma, causing significant swelling (Stromal Edema).
Step 4: Fluid migrates anteriorly through Bowman’s layer into the epithelium.
Step 5: Formation of subepithelial and intraepithelial bullae (blisters).
Step 6: Bullae rupture, exposing corneal nerves and causing intense pain and photophobia.

sections.title: Clinical Features: Symptoms & Signs
content: Symptoms: Reduced visual acuity (worse in the morning), foreign body sensation.
Symptoms: Excruciating pain and tearing upon bullae rupture.
Signs: Epithelial microcystic edema and frank bullae.
Signs: Stromal thickening and Descemet’s folds (striate keratopathy).
Signs: Subepithelial haze/fibrosis in chronic cases.
Signs: Presence of AC-IOL or vitreous in the anterior chamber (in PBK).

rows: Epithelial separation, mapping of corneal thickness
Sclerotic scatter to view subtle microcystic edema

content.explanation: P: Pleomorphism (Shape change), U: Ultra-low cell count (<500), M: Morning blurring (classic sign), P: Pachymetry (>640 um).

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: Hypertonic Saline: 5% NaCl (Muro 128) drops 4-6x daily and ointment at bedtime.
IOP Control: Beta-blockers or CAIs (Avoid Prostaglandins to minimize inflammation).
Bandage Contact Lens (BCL): For pain relief in cases of ruptured bullae.
Lubrication: Preservative-free artificial tears.
Hair Dryer Technique: Warm air (arm's length) to evaporate surface moisture in the morning.

branches: DMEK: Descemet Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty (Gold Standard)
DSAEK: Descemet Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty (Thicker tissue)
PKP: Penetrating Keratoplasty (If significant stromal scarring is present)
Gundersen Flap: For pain relief in eyes with no visual potential
DSO: Descemet Stripping Only (For central Fuchs' with good peripheral cells)

sections.title: DMEK Surgical Steps
content: Step 1: Donor membrane preparation (8-9mm DM/Endothelium strip).
Step 2: Recipient Descemetorhexis under air or viscoelastic.
Step 3: Insertion of donor roll using a glass injector (e.g., Geuder).
Step 4: Centering and unrolling using 'tapping' techniques (Melles or Dirisamer).
Step 5: Air or SF6 gas tamponade to adhere the graft.
Step 6: Post-operative supine positioning for 24-72 hours.

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Signs
content: Sudden vision loss and redness (Endophthalmitis or Graft Rejection)
Severe eye pain after BCL insertion (Possible infectious crystalline keratopathy)
IOP 'Spike' post-op (Pupillary block from air bubble)
Primary Graft Failure (Cornea remains thick and hazy after 2 weeks)

sections.title: Recent Advances: ROCK Inhibitors
content: Rho-kinase (ROCK) Inhibitors: Ripasudil/Netarsudil drops used to promote endothelial cell migration.
Endothelial Cell Injections: Cultured endothelial cells injected into the AC with the patient face-down (Kinoshita et al).
Descemet Stripping Only (DSO): Stripping central 4mm to allow peripheral cells to migrate inwards (no graft needed).
Synthetic Corneas: Evolution of keratoprosthesis (K-Pro) for multiple graft failures.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always rule out high IOP as a cause of corneal edema before diagnosing primary BK.
Specular microscopy is unreliable when the cornea is too thick (>650um) due to light scatter.
Avoid Prostaglandin Analogs (PGAs) in Fuchs' patients post-op as they may increase CME risk.
In PBK with a stable ACIOL, DSAEK is often preferred over DMEK due to easier graft manipulation.
